pharm: Essential cofactor for collagen synthesis and a reducing agent/antioxidant; corrects and prevents deficiency (scurvy).
quick: Prevention: ~75-90 mg/day (RDA). Scurvy treatment: 100-300 mg/day (or more) for several days to weeks
May be taken with or without food; with food reduces GI upset
Safe at recommended intakes (RDA ~85 mg/day); avoid megadoses
High doses risk oxalate kidney stones; caution in renal impairment/oxalosis
Resolution of deficiency; in high-dose IV settings consider oxalate/renal effects
summary: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is an essential water-soluble vitamin required for the synthesis of collagen, carnitine, and neurotransmitters, and acts as an antioxidant and reducing agent that enhances non-heme iron absorption. It is used to prevent and treat vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) and as a dietary supplement. Humans cannot synthesize it and depend on dietary intake. It is generally very safe; excess is excreted in urine, but very high doses can cause gastrointestinal upset and, with chronic use or in predisposed/renal-impaired patients, calcium oxalate kidney stones.
indications: Prevention and treatment of vitamin C deficiency (scurvy)
Dietary supplementation when intake is inadequate
Adjunct to enhance non-heme iron absorption

dosage.d: Men ~90 mg/day, women ~75 mg/day; smokers add ~35 mg/day
100-300 mg/day (commonly 250 mg several times daily) until recovery, then maintenance
100-300 mg/day in divided doses until symptoms resolve

admin: May be taken with or without food; taking with food can reduce stomach upset
Do not exceed the tolerable upper intake (~2000 mg/day in adults) without medical advice
Effervescent or chewable forms: follow product instructions
For iron-deficiency support, take together with the iron source
moa: Ascorbic acid is a cofactor for enzymes (such as prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases) essential for collagen synthesis, and for the biosynthesis of carnitine and catecholamines. As a reducing agent and antioxidant it scavenges free radicals and regenerates other antioxidants, and it reduces dietary iron to the absorbable ferrous form, enhancing non-heme iron uptake. Deficiency impairs collagen formation, producing the bleeding, poor wound healing, and connective-tissue features of scurvy.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to ascorbic acid or formulation components
relative: History of calcium oxalate kidney stones (avoid high doses)
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency (high IV doses can cause hemolysis)
Iron-overload states such as hemochromatosis or thalassemia (enhanced iron absorption)
monitor: Renal function/oxalate with chronic high doses
Hemolysis with high doses in G6PD deficiency

preg: Vitamin C is safe and needed in pregnancy at the recommended intake (about 85 mg/day); routine high-dose supplementation is unnecessary and very large doses should be avoided.
lact: Vitamin C is safe during breastfeeding at the recommended intake (about 120 mg/day) and passes into milk in normal amounts; avoid megadoses.
renal: Caution with high doses in renal impairment or a history of oxalate stones, as ascorbic acid is metabolized partly to oxalate and can promote calcium oxalate stone formation and oxalate accumulation.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required in hepatic impairment.

moderate: Iron salts (vitamin C increases iron absorption - beneficial in deficiency, caution in iron overload)
Deferoxamine (vitamin C can increase iron toxicity/cardiac risk; use cautiously)
minor: May slightly affect levels/effect of some drugs at high doses (e.g., reduced effect attributed to urinary acidification)
Estrogens/oral contraceptives (high-dose vitamin C may modestly raise estrogen levels)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; enhances absorption of non-heme iron from food.
interactions.diagnostics: High doses can cause false-negative or false-positive results in glucose tests and falsely lower/raise certain blood and stool occult-blood assays.

serious: Calcium oxalate kidney stones (chronic high doses)
Hemolysis in G6PD deficiency (high IV doses)
rare: Iron overload aggravation in predisposed patients
emergency: Acute oxalate nephropathy with very high IV doses

monitoring: Resolution of deficiency/scurvy signs (gum bleeding, bruising, wound healing)
Renal function and oxalate with chronic high-dose use
Hemolysis markers if high-dose IV in G6PD-deficient patients
counsel: A balanced diet with fruits and vegetables usually provides enough vitamin C
Very high doses are not more beneficial and can cause stomach upset, diarrhea, or kidney stones
If you have kidney stones or kidney disease, check before taking high doses
It helps your body absorb iron, so it is useful to take with iron-rich foods or supplements if advised
Stop and seek advice if you develop flank pain or blood in the urine
pk: Corrects deficiency over days to weeks of replacement
Plasma absorption is saturable; excess is excreted in urine
Body pool turns over with a biologic half-life of weeks; plasma clears faster
Maintained by ongoing dietary or supplemental intake
Store in a cool, dry place protected from light; ascorbic acid degrades with heat, light, and air
pearls: Reference-sourced (dietary reference intakes / pharmacopeial data) rather than a single openFDA drug label, as vitamin C is a nutritional supplement
Water-soluble: excess is largely excreted in urine, giving a wide safety margin
Chronic megadoses can cause calcium oxalate stones, especially with renal impairment
Enhances non-heme iron absorption - helpful in iron-deficiency anemia, but caution in iron overload
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it. Do not double up. Missing an occasional supplemental dose is not harmful.
overdose: Acute overdose typically causes only osmotic diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal discomfort, which resolve on stopping. Very large or chronic doses may cause calcium oxalate kidney stones; in G6PD deficiency, high parenteral doses can trigger hemolysis. Treatment is supportive with hydration.
